title: How Law Firms Can Lead the Agentic AI Era — And What Clients Now Expect
author: Sabastian Niles

dup.label: how law firms can lead agentic ai era what clients now expect

sib.t: How Law Firms Can Lead the Agentic AI Era — And What Clients Now Expect

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Agentic delegation: Multistep work moves verification bottlenecks
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core view that agentic legal AI depends on orchestration, workflow integration, protected context and continuing human governance rather than model capability alone. It materially extends that view by organizing deployment requirements into four interconnected systems—engagement, agency, work and context—although it supplies no measured evidence on reliability, savings or verification costs.
qs: They require four interconnected systems — engagement, agency, work, and context— all working together to create a truly Agentic Enterprise.

This requires an integrated ecosystem where agents (1) augment how lawyers uphold law as a noble profession, (2) reimagine how legal services are delivered as a business and (3) scale firm capacity to deliver elevated standards of zealous advocacy and execution, all under a strict framework of human and agent governance.

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core view that agentic AI requires operating-model and client-service redesign rather than isolated tool adoption. It materially extends that thesis by proposing unified client intelligence, AI-enabled outside-counsel workflows and direct sharing of efficiency gains with clients, while reinforcing human oversight. Its examples are company-reported and it does not resolve Harvey’s durability or the vertical-vendor versus foundation-platform contest.
qs: Heightened effectiveness and efficiency gains from AI, **shared with clients**, are no longer optional nice-to-haves; they’re prerequisites for staying competitive and seizing revenue opportunities.

- **Unified client intelligence is at the heart of legal strategy**: To take new ground and unlock significant revenue expansion through deeper cross-practice integration, law firms must move beyond point solutions to establish a single source of unified client intelligence.

st.t: Buyer transformation: Legal departments may capture AI gains
st.an: Niles accepts the cluster’s core proposition that AI gains depend on buyer-driven redesign, integrated workflows and governance rather than isolated tool adoption. He materially extends it with a four-layer agentic architecture and an explicit buyer mandate that efficiency gains be shared through savings, new business models and broader professional value, though his competitive outcomes remain predictive rather than measured.
qs: They require four interconnected systems — engagement, agency, work, and context— all working together to create a truly Agentic Enterprise.

st.t: Competitive strategy: Build-versus-buy becomes a portfolio
st.an: The source accepts that competitive advantage comes from integrated AI-enabled delivery rather than model acquisition alone, and materially extends the cluster with a buyer-side requirement: firms and ALSPs must translate governed deployment into demonstrable client value and shared efficiency gains. Its market-share predictions are forecasts, not performance evidence.
qs: Firms that don’t integrate best-in-class commercial solutions and AI will find themselves outpaced by leaner, more agile competitors.
Heightened effectiveness and efficiency gains from AI, **shared with clients**, are no longer optional nice-to-haves; they’re prerequisites for staying competitive and seizing revenue opportunities.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s emphasis on human oversight and organisational complements, while materially extending its practical deployment account through a “client zero” model, unified client intelligence and agentic administrative workflows. Its claims about talent and revenue are predictions rather than demonstrated outcomes, and it does not substantially address apprenticeship risks or profession-wide displacement.
qs: Of course, this trust is fragile, as evidenced by the near-daily reports of judicial sanctions against law firms or partners who commit the cardinal and avoidable sin of inventing citations and hallucinating precedents through lack of rigor, guardrails, and human oversight.

By becoming “client zero” —  expertly deploying a foundation for using AI in-house — firms can create a strategic client relationship vantage point, grounding their client strategy and service in collaboration, data, and operational AI fluency.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source accepts that AI will reshape legal-service delivery through buyer expectations, internal workflow integration and continued human oversight rather than displacing lawyers outright. It materially extends the cluster by identifying client-built agentic tools for outside-counsel interactions and recommending that firms act as their own first AI customer to develop integrated client intelligence and operational fluency.
qs: Some clients, like Salesforce, are even creating agentic tools to improve the law firm’s experience when working with clients.

By becoming “client zero” —  expertly deploying a foundation for using AI in-house — firms can create a strategic client relationship vantage point, grounding their client strategy and service in collaboration, data, and operational AI fluency.

st.t: Value capture: Integrated delivery reshapes market boundaries
st.an: Niles accepts the cluster’s core claim that AI value depends on integrated organisational delivery rather than isolated task efficiency, and materially develops it through a four-system agentic architecture, unified client intelligence, explicit governance and gain-sharing among providers, clients, lawyers and communities. His contribution is primarily strategic and prescriptive; it does not establish market-wide returns with quantified or independent evidence.
qs: Heightened effectiveness and efficiency gains from AI, **shared with clients**, are no longer optional nice-to-haves; they’re prerequisites for staying competitive and seizing revenue opportunities.
They require four interconnected systems — engagement, agency, work, and context— all working together to create a truly Agentic Enterprise.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core emphasis on human–AI collaboration, governance and operating-model redesign, then materially extends it with a four-layer architecture integrating engagement, agency, work and context. It is more commercially bullish and less attentive to task-level limits than the synthesis, but does not reject selective, governed deployment.
qs: This requires an integrated ecosystem where agents (1) augment how lawyers uphold law as a noble profession, (2) reimagine how legal services are delivered as a business and (3) scale firm capacity to deliver elevated standards of zealous advocacy and execution, all under a strict framework of human and agent governance.
They require four interconnected systems — engagement, agency, work, and context— all working together to create a truly Agentic Enterprise.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source endorses the cluster’s central proposition that legal delivery should be reorganised around client outcomes, buyer expectations and responsible AI integration rather than remain at the pilot or isolated-tool stage. Its Salesforce example reinforces the buyer-side adoption and competitive-pressure themes, although its broader market forecasts are asserted rather than empirically demonstrated and it does not materially address apprenticeship or pricing-model uncertainty.
qs: Firms that embrace transformation are responding to this new era with digital sophistication, competing on outcomes and setting a new global standard.
That transformation is fundamentally changing how we operate, how we govern technology, and how we partner with outside counsel.

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s account of client-driven structural pressure: it argues that firms must share AI-enabled efficiency gains with clients, predicts leaner AI-enabled competitors will outpace traditional models, and emphasises governance and human oversight. It does not directly examine junior leverage, apprenticeship or profession-wide employment effects, so its support is strongest on buyer expectations and practical adaptation.
qs: Heightened effectiveness and efficiency gains from AI, **shared with clients**, are no longer optional nice-to-haves; they’re prerequisites for staying competitive and seizing revenue opportunities.
Firms that don’t integrate best-in-class commercial solutions and AI will find themselves outpaced by leaner, more agile competitors.

st.t: Legal economics: AI makes adoption a model problem
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central view that AI adoption is a business-model and delivery-system challenge rather than a stand-alone productivity exercise. It reinforces buyer pressure to share efficiency gains and calls for integrated workflows, unified client intelligence, governance, confidentiality safeguards and human oversight. Its competitive forecasts and Salesforce examples are primarily prescriptions and company-reported claims, not quantified proof of market-wide outcomes.
qs: Heightened effectiveness and efficiency gains from AI, **shared with clients**, are no longer optional nice-to-haves; they’re prerequisites for staying competitive and seizing revenue opportunities.
We’re asking firms to move beyond experimentation and into integration.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: Niles strongly supports the cluster’s proposition that AI requires operating-model integration across workflows, data, governance and professional development, while shifting buyer expectations toward shared savings, new business models and measurable value. His competitive claims are more assertive than the cluster’s cautious synthesis and rely mainly on strategic prediction and Salesforce anecdotes, but this evidentiary limitation does not alter his overall alignment.
qs: We’re asking firms to move beyond experimentation and into integration.

st.t: Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core claim that corporate buyers are changing outside-counsel expectations and pressing firms to convert AI-enabled efficiency into client value and outcome-focused delivery. It takes a more urgent, disruption-oriented stance than the synthesis and offers strategic forecasts rather than evidence on workflow-level unbundling, pricing adoption, junior training or verification risks.
qs: Heightened effectiveness and efficiency gains from AI, **shared with clients**, are no longer optional nice-to-haves; they’re prerequisites for staying competitive and seizing revenue opportunities.
That transformation is fundamentally changing how we operate, how we govern technology, and how we partner with outside counsel.

kp.k: Client expectations make integrated AI a competitive requirement
kp.d: In this 10 March 2026 open letter, Niles argues that increasingly sophisticated legal buyers expect AI-enabled improvements in insight, speed, value and cost, rather than merely evidence of AI use. He declares experimentation insufficient and positions integration as a competitive necessity; these are buyer expectations and strategic assertions, not measured market findings.
qs: The era of the AI pilot is over.
Clients are no longer asking whether firms use AI. Rather, they’re expecting to see the benefits of that transformation passed directly to them.
They expect more for less but are not simply seeking lower costs – they want more insight, more speed, and more value for every dollar of their budget.

kp.k: AI adoption could redistribute market share and talent
kp.d: Niles applies Christensen’s innovator’s dilemma to legal services, predicting that AI-integrated firms will gain revenue, market share and talent at legacy firms’ expense. He also identifies professional service advisory firms as competitors targeting legal services. These competitive forecasts are not accompanied by market-share or hiring data.
qs: Meanwhile, professional service advisory firms worldwide have set their sights on legal services as ripe for reimagination.
Firms that don’t integrate best-in-class commercial solutions and AI will find themselves outpaced by leaner, more agile competitors.
In doing so, they will also capture the best talent, positioning themselves as the definitive employer of choice for an AI-native generation.

kp.k: In-house agentic transformation changes outside-counsel relationships
kp.d: Niles reports that Salesforce is building an AI-native, trust-first legal function and that this work is changing its operations, technology governance and outside-counsel partnerships. As a concrete example, he describes an outside-counsel support agent intended to provide consistent support and reduce e-billing friction; no quantitative outcomes are supplied.
qs: That transformation is fundamentally changing how we operate, how we govern technology, and how we partner with outside counsel.
For example, our new LCAi Outside Counsel Support Agent empowers law firms by delivering scalable, consistent support and smoothing out the legal e-billing process.
It cuts down on administrative friction and keeps our relationships with firms strong.

kp.k: Unified client intelligence supports cross-practice growth and advice
kp.d: Niles recommends replacing isolated tools with unified client intelligence grounded in secure records. He argues that internal AI deployment can enable cross-practice integration, revenue expansion and more strategic advice, while establishing credibility for advising clients on AI governance. This is a proposed organisational mechanism rather than demonstrated firm-level evidence.
qs: To take new ground and unlock significant revenue expansion through deeper cross-practice integration, law firms must move beyond point solutions to establish a single source of unified client intelligence.
To deliver strategic counsel, firms must have a 360-degree view of the client’s business and matter history.
Indeed, as we have seen in our own Customer Zero journey, the firms that master AI internally will also be the firms clients trust to govern AI externally.

kp.k: Agentic firms require four interconnected organisational systems
kp.d: Niles proposes engagement, agency, work and context as the architecture for an agentic law firm: secure collaboration interfaces; legally and ethically defensible agent behaviour; workflow-integrated enterprise infrastructure; and accurate client context protected by confidentiality, privilege and work-product safeguards. Although agents are described as acting independently at scale, their legal role is framed as augmenting lawyers under human and agent governance.
qs: Agentic AI introduces a new reality: Systems that act, decide, and execute independently at scale require more than models.
They require four interconnected systems — engagement, agency, work, and context— all working together to create a truly Agentic Enterprise.

This context must be grounded in your firm’s secure system of record, ensuring every action is informed by accurate data, protected by strict confidentiality guardrails, and architected to preserve attorney-client privilege and work-product protections.

kp.k: Human oversight and accountable governance underpin trust
kp.d: Niles cites reported judicial sanctions for invented citations and hallucinated precedents as a warning about inadequate rigour, guardrails and human oversight, without naming cases or providing a measured error rate. He recommends executive accountability for AI governance, clear oversight and risk-management rules, and privilege and confidentiality protections throughout the technology stack.
qs: Of course, this trust is fragile, as evidenced by the near-daily reports of judicial sanctions against law firms or partners who commit the cardinal and avoidable sin of inventing citations and hallucinating precedents through lack of rigor, guardrails, and human oversight.
Designate an executive sponsor responsible for AI governance and agentic workflows.
Define clear internal guardrails for the trusted use of agentic AI, including accountability, oversight, and risk management.
Affirm robust protocols to protect attorney-client privilege and client confidentiality throughout the tech stack.

kp.k: Trust assurance can enable commercial growth
kp.d: Niles presents trusted agentics as systems designed for integrity, transparency and aligned human purpose. In an undated Salesforce customer-engagement anecdote, he says addressing auditability, regulated workflows and traceable decisions converted a potential deal obstacle into a significant revenue opportunity. He generalises this to trust-dependent industries, but provides neither a transaction value nor comparative evidence.
qs: In this new era, we’re advancing trusted agentics — the discipline of designing intelligent systems that act with integrity, transparency, and aligned human purpose.
The customer asked the hard questions: How do we ensure auditable agent behavior? How do we defend regulated workflows? Where are the traceable decision paths?
We led with trust and a willingness to engage and address their concerns head-on, transforming a potential deal-blocker into a catalyst for growth and learning.

kp.k: Providers should baseline AI use and integrate workflows
kp.d: Addressing global, regional and boutique firms as well as ALSPs, Niles recommends assessing existing AI use across deliverables, service, pro bono, development and risk management. He asks providers to identify tasks agents can automate and opportunities to amplify human judgment or reduce error, then adopt secure collaboration and management platforms supporting procurement, transparent billing and scalable governance.
qs: We’re asking firms to move beyond experimentation and into integration.
Assess your firm’s current use of AI across legal deliverables, client service, pro bono impact, associate development, and risk management.
Identify where AI agents can automate tasks, scale human judgment, or reduce error to improve speed, increase quality, and uphold trust.
Law firms must adopt technologies that simplify client engagement, facilitate joint problem-solving, and streamline the procurement process.

kp.k: Efficiency gains should benefit clients and pro bono
kp.d: Niles explicitly rejects retaining AI gains solely as firm margin. He calls for savings and expanded capacity to benefit clients and communities through pro bono, alongside new business models and staff development. He predicts shared value will become both a condition of market participation and a growth differentiator, without specifying fee structures or quantifying savings or public benefit.
qs: When AI reduces time and cost, and when AI expands the capacity of your teams, those savings must be passed along to clients and invested into communities via pro bono efforts, not just used to improve firm margins.
The value that advisory firms create and unlock through agentic transformation will drive growth and can be shared with clients and communities.

kp.k: AI competence should shape professional development and promotion
kp.d: Niles recommends combining legal acumen with technical fluency across associates, counsel and partners, making AI literacy and agentic workflow competence core professional skills embedded in development and promotion. He frames transformation as a leadership challenge concerning how judgment is developed and amplified, rather than technology adoption alone.
qs: Commit to equipping associates, counsel, and partners with both legal acumen and technical fluency.
Ensure AI literacy and agentic workflow competence become core professional skills and part of all development and promotion paths.
They’ll be driven by the leaders willing to rethink how judgment is developed and amplified.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Niles predicts that integrated, responsibly governed agentic AI will reshape legal competition, client expectations, service delivery, professional skills and the distribution of efficiency gains.
pts.d: Sabastian Niles argues that AI integration is becoming a competitive prerequisite rather than an experiment. He predicts that AI-leading firms will gain revenue, market share and talent at the expense of legacy competitors. He says increasingly sophisticated clients expect efficiency gains to produce savings alongside greater insight, speed and value. Unified client intelligence and cross-practice integration are presented as sources of revenue expansion, institutional insight and stronger strategic advice; internal AI mastery is also predicted to increase clients’ trust in firms as external AI advisers. Niles describes Salesforce’s LCAi Outside Counsel Support Agent as already reducing administrative and e-billing friction. His agentic model involves systems acting independently at scale, but explicitly places legal deployment under human and agent governance and describes agents as augmenting lawyers and expanding capacity, rather than predicting wholesale lawyer replacement. He argues that trusted deployment enables expanded offerings and more efficient service, while fabricated citations and inadequate oversight threaten trust. He calls for AI savings and additional capacity to benefit clients and pro bono work, not merely firm margins, and for AI literacy and agentic workflow competence to become core development and promotion requirements.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Niles draws principally on Salesforce’s experience as a corporate legal-services buyer and AI supplier, product examples, an unnamed customer-engagement anecdote and reports of judicial sanctions.
pts.d: The letter offers an executive practitioner’s account of Salesforce’s ongoing legal-function transformation and its changing relationships with outside counsel. The LCAi support agent is a concrete operational example, but its claimed benefits are not quantified. Slackbot, Slack Connect, CRM systems and integrated platforms illustrate proposed mechanisms for collaboration and client intelligence rather than measured law-firm outcomes. Niles recounts an unnamed major customer engagement in which addressing auditability, regulated workflows and traceable decisions helped turn a potential deal obstacle into a revenue opportunity; this is an experience-based commercial example, not a legal-market study. He refers to near-daily reports of judicial sanctions for fabricated authorities without identifying cases or reporting measured model error rates. The reference to Christensen’s innovator’s dilemma supplies an interpretive analogy. No quantitative productivity results, benchmarks, market-share data, talent data or comparative studies are supplied for the broader predictions. Statements about sharing savings, pro bono investment and professional development are also buyer expectations and prescriptions, not demonstrated outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The letter frames the competitive transition as already underway in March 2026, calls for immediate integration and makes undated predictions about the next era.
pts.d: In the open letter dated 10 March 2026, Niles says experimentation should give way to integration now. Revenue, talent, service and market-share predictions concern an emerging era without quantified adoption schedules or deadlines. The gains are conditional on responsible deployment, integrated workflows and client information, accurate secure records, confidentiality and privilege protections, and accountable human and agent governance. Sharing savings is expressly conditional on AI reducing time and cost or expanding capacity. Niles treats trust as essential to competitive advantage, not an automatic consequence of AI adoption. His specific near-term commitment is to convene conversations and share playbooks, governance frameworks, best practices and learning paths in the coming months.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims address legal providers of multiple sizes, corporate buyers, lawyers and firm leaders, competing advisory businesses, and communities benefiting from pro bono work.
pts.d: Global and regional firms, boutiques and ALSPs are invited to integrate agentic capabilities and share gains. Traditional providers face predicted competitive losses, while leaner AI-leading providers are expected to gain work and talent; professional-service advisory firms are described as targeting legal services, without naming particular entrants. Corporate clients, including Salesforce, are positioned as increasingly demanding buyers seeking savings, speed, insight, transparent billing and better collaboration. Associates, counsel and partners are expected to acquire technical fluency, develop judgment and use expanded capacity; the letter does not provide staffing-reduction or junior-displacement forecasts. Firm leaders and executive sponsors are assigned governance responsibilities. Communities are intended beneficiaries through expanded pro bono impact, distinct from corporate cost savings. Niles also attributes to law firms wider influence over trusted AI deployment across industries.
